summary.text: Electronegativity is how strongly an atom of an element attracts shared electrons when it forms a chemical bond.
It cannot be measured directly, so it is calculated from other properties, most commonly on the Pauling scale that Linus Pauling proposed in 1932.
Differences in electronegativity estimate a bond's energy and polarity, placing it on a scale from covalent to ionic.

items.prompt: Why did Pauling need a reference point when building his scale?

options.label: Because the scale only exists for hydrogen compounds
Because only differences in electronegativity are defined
Because every element had already been measured exactly
Because bond energies cannot be used to compare atoms

items.explain: Since only differences are defined, an arbitrary reference point had to be chosen, and hydrogen was picked because it forms covalent bonds with many elements.

items.prompt: Pauling noticed a bond between two different atoms was stronger than the average of the two matching same-atom bonds. What did he offer to explain it?

options.label: The idea of electronegativity
A drop in the number of protons
A sea of electrons shared by all atoms
The lattice energy of the crystal

items.explain: Pauling first proposed electronegativity in 1932 to explain why the covalent bond between two different atoms is stronger than the average of the A-A and B-B bonds.

items.prompt: The same atom shows up in two different molecules. What does the use of electronegativity assume?

options.label: Its value must be random each time
Its value is exactly the same in every molecule
Its value is usually treated as transferable between situations
Its value only applies to the atom when it is alone

items.explain: Electronegativity varies with chemical environment, but it is usually considered transferable, with similar values valid in a variety of situations.

paragraphs.heading: A pull on shared electrons
paragraphs.text: Electronegativity, written with the Greek letter χ, describes how strongly an atom draws in the electrons it shares with another atom in a chemical bond. The higher an atom's value, the harder it pulls. Its loosely defined opposite is electropositivity, which describes how readily an element gives away its valence electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Why chemists use it
paragraphs.text: Electronegativity gives a simple numerical way to estimate how much energy a bond holds. It also gives the direction and the size of a bond's polarity. With that, any bond can be placed somewhere on a continuous scale that runs from covalent bonding to ionic bonding. An atom's value depends on its atomic number and on how far its valence electrons sit from the charged nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: An old idea, a late scale
paragraphs.text: The word was introduced by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1811, though chemists such as Avogadro had studied the idea before then. Even so, no accurate scale existed until 1932. That year Linus Pauling proposed one based on bond energies. He wanted to explain why a covalent A–B bond, linking two different atoms, is stronger than the A–A and B–B bonds averaged together.

paragraphs.heading: The Pauling scale
paragraphs.text: Electronegativity cannot be measured directly; it has to be calculated from other properties of atoms or molecules. Pauling's method is still the one most often used. It gives a number with no units, on a relative scale from 0.79 to 3.98. Caesium sits at the bottom at 0.79 and fluorine at the top at 3.98. Hydrogen is the reference point: Pauling first set it at 0, then at 2.1 to avoid negative figures, and Allred later revised it to 2.20.

paragraphs.heading: Many methods, one pattern
paragraphs.text: Several other ways of calculating electronegativity have been proposed. Their numbers can differ a little, but every method shows the same periodic trends between the elements. By custom, though not by rule, results from other methods are quoted over the same range as Pauling's, in what are called Pauling units. One alternative, the Mulliken electronegativity, can only be worked out for an element whose electron affinity is known.

paragraphs.heading: An atom in a molecule
paragraphs.text: As it is usually calculated, electronegativity belongs to an atom inside a molecule rather than to an atom on its own. It should shift with an atom's chemical surroundings, and this adds error in more complex compounds. Still, it is usually treated as transferable, meaning similar values work in a variety of situations. It is also strongly linked to an atom's first ionization energy.

paragraphs.heading: Which atom pulls harder
paragraphs.text: A scale still needs a decision about which of two bonded atoms is the more electronegative one. This is often settled by chemical intuition. Hydrogen bromide, for example, dissolves in water to give H⁺ and Br⁻ ions. From that, it is reasonable to assume that bromine pulls on electrons more strongly than hydrogen does.
